The five tier-1 providers, in the accent color, form a full clique at the top; the mid-level providers, in teal, and the content provider, in a third color, sit in the middle row; and the customers, in a fourth color, sit along the bottom. Customers buy transit from the providers above them, and edges between two nodes of the same kind, the peering links, take its color." width="100%"} The model of Elmokashfi, Kvalbein and Dovrolis (2010) builds an internet-like graph of `n` autonomous systems (AS) of four kinds, stored as each node's `type`: - `"T"`: a handful (4 to 6) of tier-1 transit providers, all peering with each other - `"M"`: mid-level providers (about 15% of the nodes), customers of T or other M nodes - `"CP"`: content providers (about 5%), customers that also peer with M and CP nodes - `"C"`: customer networks (the rest), at the edge of the network Nodes live in five geographic regions and pick their providers inside their own region(s), by preferential attachment on degree. Each edge's `rel` attribute records the relationship: `"transit"` for a customer buying transit from a provider, and `"peer"` for two networks exchanging traffic as equals. A transit edge runs from the customer to its provider, so its `source` is the customer (in an undirected graph too). The process is NetworkX's `random_internet_as_graph()`, which instead stores the customer in a `customer` edge attribute. NetworkX can create more than `n` nodes when `n < 8`; here the M and CP counts are capped so there are always exactly `n`. Peer edges point from the earlier-created node to the later one in a directed graph. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Internet AS graphs are useful for: - studying routing, resilience and attacks on internet-like topologies - testing algorithms on hierarchical networks with typed nodes and edges - simulating how traffic or failures propagate along customer-provider chains ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of autonomous systems. Must be non-negative. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same other arguments always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the graph differs on every call. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` is negative. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A 1000-node internet has a few tier-1 providers and mostly customer networks: ::: {#776d75c5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_random_internet_as_graph(n=1000, seed=3) graph.get_node_df()["type"].value_counts().sort("type") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

typecount

"CP"50
"M"150
"T"5
``` ::: ::: Most edges are transit links from a customer to its provider: ::: {#e2c0b587 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_edge_df()["rel"].value_counts().sort("rel") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
